title: White popularisers and uncredited Black arrangers
summary: Gitler and Hall discuss white players who profited from bebop and arrangers writing without credit.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Of course, after, you know, in the days of 52nd Street, and when, you know, the music, despite all the negative criticism began to be -- become the new expression and the new thing of that era, then, of course, I'm not talking about the white musicians who played with these bands like Al Haig and people like that, Red Rodney and what have you, but came behind that when they saw a dollar was to be made with it perhaps. Then white bands started playing in this -- in this style.
You know, they became the so called popularizers, you know, the Charlie Venturas and the George Shearings and, et cetera, et cetera. You know.

Well -- well, let me put it this way. When the Charlie Venturas and Red Rodneys and whatnot started playing with the Black musicians, then if there was a job open, they would become a leader of something important and go from there.

But Teddy Wilson never got that opportunity, and Art Tatum was blind, Sy Oliver should have done it. Don Redman -- these people had credits, you know. But what they were doing was writing for the white show without getting the

credits, because I was a copyist, and I copied a lot of these, Don Redman's things and Sy Oliver's and Luther Henderson's and for -- for name bands -- Eddie Barefield, Joe Garaggiola -- not Joe Garaggiola -- Joe Cordilla, the clarinetist. He used to be with Whiteman,
Man, his music was just -- he played so many notes. That's why I'm wearing glasses, to try to read his music.
